title: What Louis taught Moore about performing
summary: Armstrong gave subtle pointers on solos and projection; Moore says they never had a cross word.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: But the job was really hard. because he had to get up early and make the two performances. So after the Zanzibar we went on tour practically all over the country, up through Canada and way out to the west coast, south -- oh, all over and so my days with Louie there was a wonderful experience. I learned quite a bit through Louie because he would tell me different -- real subtle like, "Chief, why don't you -- when I play my solos," and he would tell me, "Why don't you do this, come in at this period because you want to save your chops for this part here and when you come about here, you sing over here," and he would give me pointers that way. I always agreed with him and did whatever -- when he would tell

me, I never took the initiative and say, "Don't tell me, I'm the -- I can't do that stuff --" not to a man like Louis, he's so congenial and so great and he taught me a lot of stuff, things about performance and projection. It was beautiful just to be with him. Louie and I never had a cross word. He's the same on the bandstand and he's the same off the bandstand, too, and all the guys in the band respected him at that time, in fact all the time. I didn't see anybody that had any words with him, we respected him as a leader and as a musician and on top of all, a human being. He treated everybody the same way. I'd say that he'd been in the music business all his life up to that point, he's Mr. Experience. We could tell that he's one of the greatest.
